title: Protein Binding and Allostery: How Hemoglobin Loads and Delivers Oxygen

generated.pipeline: extract → Opus draft → Sonnet accuracy gate → Sonnet fixes

cards.front: What is the approximate pO₂ in the lungs, in blood leaving resting tissue, and in blood leaving hard-working muscle?
cards.back: About 100 torr in the lungs, about 40 torr leaving resting tissue, and about 20 torr leaving hard-working muscle.
cards.quote: Blood leaving resting tissue is near 40 torr, and blood leaving hard-working muscle is near 20 torr.
cards.section: The delivery problem: load in the lungs, unload in the tissues

cards.front: Why would an O₂ carrier that binds oxygen more tightly than hemoglobin deliver less oxygen, not more?
cards.back: It fills in the lungs but is still nearly full at muscle pO₂, and oxygen that stays bound is not delivered.
cards.quote: A tight binder fills up in the lungs, but it is still nearly full when it reaches the muscle, and oxygen that stays aboard is not delivered.
cards.section: The delivery problem: load in the lungs, unload in the tissues

cards.front: In the two-state picture of hemoglobin, what sets how full hemoglobin is at a given pO₂?
cards.back: The average of how full the T shape and the R shape would each be, weighted by the fraction of molecules in each shape.
cards.quote: How full hemoglobin is at any pO₂ is the average of how full each shape would be, weighted by how much of each shape is present.
cards.section: The delivery problem: load in the lungs, unload in the tissues

cards.front: Which ligands shift hemoglobin's T/R mix toward R, and which toward T?
cards.back: Toward R: O₂ and CO. Toward T: H⁺, CO₂ and 2,3-BPG.
cards.quote: Oxygen and CO favor R; H⁺, CO₂ and 2,3-BPG favor T.
cards.section: The delivery problem: load in the lungs, unload in the tissues

cards.front: For the dissociation reaction RL ⇌ R + L, the dissociation constant is Kd = {{c1::[R][L] / [RL]}}.
cards.back: Loose over bound; units of concentration.
cards.quote: The dissociation constant is the ratio of what is loose to what is bound
cards.section: One site: Kd and the hyperbola

cards.front: How are Kd and Ka related, and which direction means tighter binding for each?
cards.back: Ka = 1/Kd. A smaller Kd means tighter binding; a bigger Ka means tighter binding.
cards.quote: Kd is not Ka, the association constant, which is its reciprocal (Ka = 1/Kd, so a bigger Ka means tighter binding).
cards.section: One site: Kd and the hyperbola

cards.front: Why does Kd equal the free ligand concentration at which a single site is half occupied?
cards.back: At half occupancy [R] = [RL], so they cancel in Kd = [R][L]/[RL], leaving Kd = [L].
cards.why: So a small Kd means very little ligand fills half the sites: tight binding.
cards.quote: At that point the bound and free receptor populations are equal, [R] = [RL], and they cancel
cards.section: Why Kd is the concentration at half-saturation

cards.front: A single-site receptor (no cooperativity, ligand in excess) has Kd = 10 nM. What free ligand concentrations give 75% and 90% occupancy?
cards.back: Y = [L]/(Kd + [L]). Y = 0.75 when [L] = 3 × Kd = 30 nM; Y = 0.9 when [L] = 9 × Kd = 90 nM.
cards.why: Going from half full to 90% full takes nine times the Kd: the slow bend of the hyperbola.
cards.quote: Going from half full to 90% full takes nine times as much ligand.
cards.section: Why Kd is the concentration at half-saturation

cards.front: Why is a single site's P50 for oxygen the same thing as its Kd, expressed in torr?
cards.back: Dissolved O₂ concentration is proportional to its partial pressure, so the pO₂ at half-saturation stands in for the ligand concentration at half-saturation.
cards.quote: Oxygen is a gas, and the concentration of a dissolved gas is proportional to its partial pressure.

cards.front: What is the shape of myoglobin's O₂-binding curve, and its approximate P50?
cards.back: A plain hyperbola (non-cooperative, one site), with a P50 of about 2 torr.
cards.quote: Its binding curve is a plain hyperbola, the same shape as the Kd plot, with a P50 of about 2 torr.

cards.front: Myoglobin (P50 about 2 torr, hyperbolic) is about 98% saturated at 100 torr. Estimate its saturation at 20 torr and the fraction of O₂ it would unload between 100 and 20 torr.
cards.back: Y = 20 / (2 + 20) ≈ 0.91, so about 91% full. Unloaded ≈ 98 − 91 = about 7%.
cards.why: 20 torr is far above its P50, so the site stays nearly always occupied; this suits a storage protein.
cards.quote: Twenty torr is far above its P50, so the site is still nearly always occupied.

cards.front: In hemoglobin, how do the T and R shapes differ in structure and in O₂ affinity?
cards.back: T (tense) has extra salt bridges between subunits and binds O₂ weakly; R (relaxed) has fewer bridges and binds O₂ tightly.
cards.quote: T (tense) is held together by extra salt bridges (attractions between oppositely charged side chains) between the subunits.

cards.front: Does hemoglobin need bound oxygen to adopt the R shape?
cards.back: No. Even with no O₂ it flickers between T and R, but T is so much more stable that R molecules are almost absent.
cards.quote: Even with no oxygen at all, it flickers between T and R, but T is so much more stable that R molecules are almost absent.

cards.front: Hypothetical two-state carrier at one pO₂: half the molecules are R. An R site would be 99% full and a T site 25% full at that pO₂. What is the overall saturation?
cards.why: The rule averages how full each shape is, weighted by population.
cards.quote: Ask how full each shape would be on its own, then average, counting each shape in proportion to how much of it there is.

cards.front: Why does binding oxygen shift hemoglobin's T ⇌ R balance toward R?
cards.back: R holds O₂ far more tightly, so each bound O₂ makes R more favorable relative to T: Le Chatelier's principle applied to shape.
cards.quote: R holds oxygen far more tightly, so every oxygen bound makes R a little more favorable compared with T.

cards.front: In an illustrative two-state fit of hemoglobin, an R site is half full at about 0.37 torr and a T site at about 110 torr. By what factor does each bound O₂ multiply the odds that the molecule is R?
cards.why: The factor equals how much more tightly R holds oxygen than T does.
cards.quote: Each oxygen multiplies the odds of R by the same large factor, about 300 in this fit (110 / 0.37)

cards.front: In the two-state picture, why is hemoglobin's O₂ curve flat at low pO₂, steep in the middle and flat again near full?
cards.back: Low pO₂: nearly all T, so the curve follows T's weak hyperbola. Middle: each bound O₂ tips molecules into R, whose empty sites fill easily. High pO₂: nearly all R, near full.
cards.quote: Through the middle each bound oxygen tips more molecules into R, and an R molecule's empty sites are suddenly easy to fill.

cards.front: A four-site protein has two shapes, but both shapes bind O₂ with the same affinity. What shape is its binding curve, and why?
cards.back: A plain hyperbola (in the two-state model, Hill coefficient exactly 1). Oxygen gives neither shape an advantage, so the mix never shifts.
cards.why: An S needs two shapes that differ in affinity plus a ligand that shifts the mix between them.
cards.quote: If both shapes bind equally, oxygen gives neither an advantage, so the mix never shifts, and the curve is just one single-site curve.

cards.front: In the two-state picture, how are hemoglobin's four binding sites coupled without a separate message passing between subunits?
cards.back: They share one overall shape, carried across the subunit contacts, so whatever shifts that shape changes all four sites at once.
cards.quote: the four sites are coupled because they share one overall shape, carried across the contacts between the subunits

cards.front: Human hemoglobin's Hill coefficient is about 2.8. Does that mean about 2.8 sites cooperate? What does it measure, and what limits it?
cards.back: No. It scores the steepness of the curve at half-saturation. It is 1 for independent sites and can be no larger than the number of sites (4 for hemoglobin).
cards.quote: It can be no larger than the number of sites, so 4 for hemoglobin.

cards.front: Hemoglobin's P50 is about {{c1::26 torr}}, against myoglobin's 2 torr.
cards.quote: Hemoglobin's P50 is about 26 torr, against myoglobin's 2.

cards.front: A non-cooperative carrier (n_H = 1) has hemoglobin's P50 of 26 torr. What fraction of its O₂ does it deliver between 100 and 20 torr?
cards.back: Y = pO₂/(P50 + pO₂). At 100 torr: 100/126 ≈ 0.79. At 20 torr: 20/46 ≈ 0.43. Delivered ≈ 0.36, about 36%, versus about two-thirds for hemoglobin.
cards.quote: Where the steep part sits matters just as much, and P50 sets that.

cards.front: A carrier is as cooperative as hemoglobin (n_H = 2.8) but has myoglobin's P50 of 2 torr. How much O₂ does it deliver between 100 and 20 torr, and why?
cards.back: Almost none. Its steep part sits far below 20 torr, so it is still nearly full in working muscle.
cards.why: A good carrier needs an S whose steep part sits between lung and muscle pressures.
cards.quote: a steep curve in the wrong place delivers almost nothing, because it is still nearly full at 20 torr.

cards.front: Two purified O₂-binding proteins (made-up data). Protein P: 99% saturated at 100 torr, 94% at 20 torr. Protein Q: 97% at 100 torr, 33% at 20 torr. Which behaves like a delivery carrier and which like a storage protein?
cards.back: Q is the carrier: it unloads about 64% between 100 and 20 torr, so its steep part lies between those pressures. P unloads about 5%, like high-affinity myoglobin.
cards.quote: Hemoglobin needs both: an S, and an S whose steep part sits between the lungs and the muscle.

cards.front: In heme, the iron makes four bonds to the porphyrin nitrogens, a fifth to the {{c1::proximal histidine}}, and saves its sixth coordination site for oxygen.
cards.quote: holds a fifth bond to a histidine reaching up from the protein (the proximal histidine), and saves its sixth coordination site for oxygen

cards.front: What happens to hemoglobin if its heme iron is oxidized from Fe²⁺ to Fe³⁺?
cards.back: It becomes methemoglobin, which cannot carry oxygen at all.
cards.quote: The iron must stay Fe²⁺; oxidize it to Fe³⁺ and you get methemoglobin, which cannot carry oxygen at all.

cards.front: Why does the heme iron sit about 0.4 Å out of the porphyrin plane in deoxyhemoglobin, and why does it move into the plane on O₂ binding?
cards.back: Deoxy iron is high-spin and slightly too big for the porphyrin hole. O₂ binding makes it low-spin, so it shrinks and moves into the plane.
cards.quote: In the deoxy T state the iron is high-spin and slightly too big to fit the porphyrin hole, so it sits about 0.4 Å out of the ring plane, on the side of the proximal histidine.

cards.front: How does the sub-ångström drop of the heme iron on O₂ binding become hemoglobin's T-to-R switch?
cards.back: The iron pulls the proximal histidine, which shifts the F helix against the neighboring subunit; this levers a roughly 15° rotation of one αβ dimer against the other, and T's salt bridges break.
cards.why: Read backwards: in T those salt bridges resist the movements, so O₂ binding is less favorable there.
cards.quote: The twitch at the iron is levered into roughly a 15° rotation of one αβ dimer against the other, and the salt bridges that held the T state break.

cards.front: By the two-state rule, what does any molecule that binds hemoglobin's T state better than R do to the O₂ curve?
cards.back: It shifts the mix toward T, so more O₂ is needed to tip it to R: the curve moves right, P50 rises and affinity falls.
cards.quote: If it binds T better than R, it shifts the mix toward T, so it takes more oxygen to tip the population to R

cards.front: Where does 2,3-BPG bind on hemoglobin?
cards.back: In a central pocket between the β chains that is wide open only in the T state.
cards.quote: It wedges into a central pocket between the β chains that is wide open only in the T state

cards.front: A person moves to high altitude and red-cell 2,3-BPG rises over hours to days. What happens to hemoglobin's P50 and to O₂ release at a given tissue pO₂?
cards.back: P50 rises (right shift), and more O₂ is released at a given tissue pO₂.
cards.why: BPG binds and holds the T state, so more O₂ is needed to tip the mix to R; this is part of acclimatization.
cards.quote: It rises in your red cells over hours to days at high altitude, which is part of how you acclimatize

cards.front: What is the Bohr effect, and how does low pH lower hemoglobin's O₂ affinity?
cards.back: Protons lower O₂ affinity. Protonated groups, chiefly a histidine near the end of each β chain, form salt bridges that steady the T state.
cards.quote: Protonating certain groups on hemoglobin, chiefly a histidine near the end of each β chain, lets them form salt bridges that steady the T state

cards.front: How does CO₂ bind hemoglobin directly, and which shape does it favor?
cards.back: As carbamate groups on hemoglobin's N-termini, which form T-stabilizing salt bridges.
cards.quote: Carbon dioxide binds as carbamate groups (CO₂ bonded to an amino group) on hemoglobin's N-termini, which form their own T-stabilizing salt bridges.

cards.front: During exercise, working muscle has falling pO₂, falling pH and rising CO₂. What happens to O₂ unloading there, and why?
cards.back: More O₂ is unloaded. Low pO₂ moves down the curve, and H⁺ and CO₂ both stabilize T, shifting the curve right exactly where O₂ is needed.
cards.quote: During exercise, three fast signals arrive at once in working muscle: falling pO₂, falling pH and rising CO₂.

cards.front: Right-shifting hemoglobin's O₂ curve lowers affinity. Why do H⁺, CO₂ and a modest BPG rise not spoil O₂ loading in the lungs?
cards.back: H⁺ and CO₂ are high in tissue, not lungs, so their shift acts where unloading happens. BPG shifts the curve everywhere, but the lung end lies on the flat top, so a modest shift costs little loading.
cards.quote: H⁺ and CO₂ are high in tissue, not in the lungs, so their shift happens where unloading happens.

cards.front: In the two-state fit of hemoglobin, tripling T's advantage raises delivery (100 to 20 torr) from about 64% to 71%. Predict whether a tenfold increase helps more, and why.
cards.back: No. P50 moves to about 48 torr and delivery falls back to about 66%, because the curve no longer fills fully at 100 torr.
cards.why: A right shift helps only while the lung end stays on the flat top of the curve.
cards.quote: A tenfold increase moves P50 to about 48 torr, and delivery falls back from 71% to about 66%, because the curve no longer fills fully at 100 torr.

cards.front: Why does fetal hemoglobin (α₂γ₂) have higher O₂ affinity than adult hemoglobin, and what does that allow?
cards.back: Its γ chain has serine where adult β has histidine at position 143, so it binds 2,3-BPG weakly. Less BPG holds it in T, so it pulls O₂ across the placenta from maternal blood.
cards.quote: With less BPG holding it in T, it stays at higher oxygen affinity and pulls oxygen across the placenta from the mother's blood.

cards.front: A hypothetical adult hemoglobin carries a β143 His→Ser substitution, as in the fetal γ chain. Predict its P50 and its O₂ release to working muscle.
cards.back: Lower P50 (left shift, higher affinity) and less O₂ released to tissue.
cards.why: By the fetal hemoglobin rule, serine at 143 weakens BPG binding, so less BPG holds the molecule in T.
cards.quote: Fetal hemoglobin (α₂γ₂) has a serine where the adult β chain has a histidine at position 143, so it binds 2,3-BPG weakly.

cards.front: How much more tightly does CO bind hemoglobin's heme than O₂, and which shape does it favor?
cards.back: About 250-fold more tightly; like O₂, it favors R.
cards.quote: It binds the heme about 250-fold more tightly than oxygen does, and like oxygen it favors R.
cards.section: When the shapes betray you: hemoglobin pathology

cards.front: A hemoglobin tetramer carries CO on one subunit and O₂ on the other three. How tightly are those three O₂ held, and why is CO poisoning a double harm?
cards.back: More tightly than usual: CO locks the tetramer in high-affinity R, shifting the curve left. Fewer sites carry O₂, and the O₂ carried is not released in tissue.
cards.quote: That is double damage: fewer sites carry oxygen, and the oxygen that is carried stays put in the tissues.
cards.section: When the shapes betray you: hemoglobin pathology

cards.front: A patient with CO poisoning is checked with a pulse oximeter. What does it read, and why?
cards.back: Falsely normal, while tissues are starved of O₂, because the oximeter cannot tell O₂-hemoglobin from CO-hemoglobin.
cards.quote: A pulse oximeter, which cannot tell O₂-hemoglobin from CO-hemoglobin, reads falsely normal while tissues suffocate.
cards.section: When the shapes betray you: hemoglobin pathology

cards.front: Sickle-cell hemoglobin carries a {{c1::glutamate-to-valine}} substitution at position 6 of the β chain.
cards.back: Glu6→Val.
cards.quote: Glutamate to valine, at position 6 of the β chain.
cards.section: When the shapes betray you: hemoglobin pathology

cards.front: Val6 of sickle hemoglobin is on the surface in every state. Why does HbS polymerize only when deoxygenated?
cards.back: The hydrophobic pocket Val6 docks into (Phe85, Leu88) on a neighboring hemoglobin is open only in the deoxy T shape, so molecules chain into fibers only in T.
cards.quote: That valine sits on the surface in every state, but the hydrophobic pocket it docks into (Phe85, Leu88) on a neighboring hemoglobin is open only in the deoxy T shape.
cards.section: When the shapes betray you: hemoglobin pathology

cards.front: Why do exertion, cold and dehydration each promote sickling crises?
cards.back: Exertion (more O₂ use) and cold (slower flow in small vessels) leave more hemoglobin in T for longer. Dehydration concentrates HbS, so fibers form faster.
cards.quote: Exertion and cold leave more hemoglobin in T for longer.
cards.section: When the shapes betray you: hemoglobin pathology

cards.front: In a person with sickle-cell disease, working muscle becomes acidic and CO₂-rich. Predict the effect on sickling in that tissue, and the rule it rests on.
cards.back: Sickling is promoted. H⁺ and CO₂ stabilize T, and only in T is the pocket open that lets Val6 of one HbS molecule plug into the next.
cards.quote: So in T, the valine of one molecule plugs into the pocket of the next, which plugs into the next.
cards.section: When the shapes betray you: hemoglobin pathology

cards.front: Why does switching fetal hemoglobin back on in red-cell precursors (as the CRISPR therapy Casgevy does) reduce sickling?
cards.back: HbF does not join the sickle polymer and dilutes the HbS around it, so cells sickle far less.
cards.quote: HbF does not join the sickle polymer and dilutes the HbS around it, so cells sickle far less.
cards.section: When the shapes betray you: hemoglobin pathology

cards.front: In α-thalassemia, surplus β chains form β₄ tetramers (HbH) that bind O₂ tightly with no cooperativity. Predict how well HbH delivers O₂ between lungs and working muscle.
cards.back: Poorly. It binds tightly with no cooperativity, so it holds on to O₂ rather than releasing it in muscle.
cards.why: Rests on the delivery rule: delivery needs an S whose steep part lies between 100 and 20 torr.
cards.quote: bind oxygen tightly but with no cooperativity, a delivery truck that forgot how to open its doors
